summary: BBN's monthly traffic statistics for the ARPANET hosts for December 1972, shown as tables of packets output per host, including traffic between sites and within a site. A few days of data were missing. It updates RFC 422 and is a record of usage, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card counting how many messages each computer on the network sent in one month.

questions: how much data did early arpanet use
subtitle: The ARPANET's usage statistics showing traffic across all connected systems in December 1972.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET community needed to understand how the network was being used and how much traffic different sites were generating.
tldr.mechanism: BBN collected and published monthly traffic statistics showing the number of packets output by each host, broken down into inter-node (between sites) and intra-node (within a site) traffic.
tldr.outcome: A monthly report that documents ARPANET usage patterns and provides baseline data for understanding the network's growth and operation.

today: This RFC is a historical document showing ARPANET usage patterns in early 1973. Regular traffic statistics remain important for network management, but modern networks have far more sophisticated monitoring and telemetry systems that track usage in real-time across billions of devices.

sections.title: Network Traffic Statistics
sections.content:
RFC 443 presents the ARPANET's host traffic statistics for December 1972, compiled and published by BBN. The report shows how much data each connected host was transmitting, measured in packets. The data is presented in a table format showing each site and its hosts, with columns for inter-node traffic (packets sent to other sites), intra-node traffic (packets sent locally), and daily averages.

This was a regular monthly report that the community relied on to track network usage and understand which sites and applications were most active.
sections.plainLanguage: A monthly scorecard showing how busy each computer was on the network.

sections.title: The Data
sections.content:
The report includes traffic data from about 25 sites connected to the ARPANET in December 1972, including UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UCSB, University of Utah, BBN, MIT, Rand, Harvard, MIT Lincoln Labs, Stanford, University of Illinois, Carnegie Mellon, NASA Ames, and others. Some nodes had no traffic, either because they were inactive or not yet connected.

The top traffic generators included Ames Research Center, ISI, BBN, Stanford, and MIT. The total inter-node traffic for the month exceeded 28 million packets, with a daily average of about 1.1 million packets, or about 34,000 packets per node per day. The report notes that some days of data were missing due to collection problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest computers sending messages were at space agencies and research labs. The whole network sent tens of millions of messages in one month.

sections.title: A Snapshot of Early ARPANET Usage
sections.content:
These statistics capture the ARPANET at a specific moment in its growth, about four years after the first IMP installation. The data reveals which sites were most active participants and shows the relative balance of traffic across different types of institutions. The distinction between inter-node and intra-node traffic indicates that many sites had multiple hosts and generated significant local traffic.

Regular publication of these reports became an important part of network management, providing the community with visibility into how the network was being used and helping coordinate growth and upgrades.
sections.plainLanguage: This shows what the early network looked like in December 1972, which computers were busy, and how much they were talking to each other.
